title: Working Memory Theory
subtitle: Why dual attention may reduce vividness and distress
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating working memory theory across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain working memory theory in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in working memory theory.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to working memory theory.

sections.explainSimply: Holding a distressing image in mind while doing another demanding task can tax limited working-memory resources.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Competition may make the recalled image temporarily less vivid and emotional, enabling new appraisal or updating.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Laboratory effects are reproducible for eye movements and other taxing tasks, but they do not alone explain all clinical outcomes of EMDR.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of working memory theory as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need working memory theory to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Reducing vividness is not the same as resolving meaning or risk.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use working memory theory to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses working memory theory to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Reducing vividness is not the same as resolving meaning or risk. Evidence classification: promising mechanism with experimental support.
